title: Schedule at Certain Time + Recurring Tasks
summary: One-shot and recurring schedules are promises to fire on user intent, not cron rows. Store the intent, expand occurrences just-in-time, and make firing idempotent.
topic: User Empathy, User Experience, Future Proofing & Realistic Design

blocks.title: The one idea that matters
blocks.text: A schedule is **a promise to fire at a human-meaningful moment despite restarts, edits, DST, and retries**. If you store `next_fire_at` as a dumb timestamp and poll it, you have built a bug, not a scheduler. Store **intent** (`09:00 in America/Chicago, every weekday`), derive fires deterministically, and make every fire **idempotent**. The trade-off: you pay complexity in expansion logic to buy correctness when everything else fails.
What "schedule at a time" actually means

Precisely: a user declares an **intent** — `run once at T` or `run repeatedly per rule R starting at T` — and the system must produce **occurrences** that fire within seconds of the user's expectation, exactly once in effect, even across deploys, crashes, timezone moves, and edits to the series. An occurrence has four states: `scheduled`, `due`, `fired`, and `cancelled`. A recurring task is not N copies of a one-shot task. It is **one template plus a deterministic expansion function** plus a sparse set of **overrides**. Confuse the template with the occurrences and every follow-up — skip one instance, reschedule the series, change timezone, delete future but keep past — becomes a data migration. Separate them and those operations are single-row writes. That separation is why interviewers ask this: it tests whether you design for mutation, not just creation.

One-shot and recurring look identical at fire time but diverge everywhere else. A one-shot has no expansion, no DST recurrence problem, and deletion is trivial. A recurring task has unbounded future, user edits that apply retroactively vs. going forward, and per-instance state (`done`, `skipped`, `snoozed`). The correct model is: `RecurringSchedule{id, user_id, rrule, start_at, timezone, end_condition}` owns `Occurrence{series_id, occurrence_id, scheduled_for, status, idempotency_key}` where `occurrence_id` is deterministic like `series_id#2026-09-07`. The trade-off is storage vs. computation: you never persist the infinite series, you persist the rule and materialize a bounded window of occurrences. That is what lets you show a calendar, allow check-offs, and survive rule changes without rewriting history.
The mechanism: never store the fires

blocks.title: Schedule intent to fire pipeline
blocks.caption: Intent is stored once, expanded to a bounded window, then claimed idempotently at fire time.
blocks.code:
flowchart LR
  Client["Client API"] --> Svc["Schedule Service"]
  Svc --> Store[("Schedule Store")] 
  Store --> Expander["Expander"]
  Expander --> Window[("Occurrence Window")] 
  Window --> Queue["Delayed Queue"]
  Queue --> Worker["Fire Worker"]
  Worker --> Outbox[("Outbox + Idempotency")] 
  Outbox --> Notify["Notifier / Push"]

blocks.text: The write path stores intent and validates it synchronously: parse the `RRULE`, reject impossible rules, normalize to UTC **plus** retain the original wall-clock and timezone. The read path for calendars expands the rule for the requested window only — typically now to now plus 30 to 90 days — and merges overrides. The fire path is separate: a dispatcher scans the materialized window for `due <= now+lookahead`, enqueues `(occurrence_id, fire_at)` into a delayed queue, and workers **claim by lease** before notifying. Why this split? Because correctness and latency have opposite needs. Intent storage must be strongly consistent and auditable; firing must be highly available and retry-safe. Coupling them — firing directly from the schedule table with `SELECT * WHERE next_fire < now` — forces your database to be both source of truth and job queue, which is why it collapses under load and double-fires on failover. The trade-off: an extra queue and claim protocol buys you at-most-once claiming with at-least-once delivery, which composes to effectively-once effect via idempotency keys.
Expansion: the core decision

blocks.caption: How you turn a rule into occurrences determines scale and editability.
rows: Pre-materialize all
Insert N rows up front for a year of dailies
Trivial queries, trivial per-instance state
Explodes on edit: rescheduling 50 meetings rewrites 50 rows; unbounded rules impossible
Just-in-time expansion
Compute on read from RRULE, persist nothing per instance
Zero write amplification, edits are free
Cannot attach state to an instance; calendar pagination and search get expensive
Bounded hybrid
Materialize 30-90 day window, roll forward with a sweeper
Calendar is fast, edits touch only window, history stays immutable
Needs a roller and reconciliation; more moving parts to operate

blocks.text: Choose the hybrid for anything human-facing. It is the only option that survives the realistic follow-up: *user moves Monday standup from 09:00 to 10:00 for all future instances*. With pre-materialization you run a bulk update that races with firers. With pure JIT you have nowhere to record that last Monday was skipped. With a bounded window you update the template once, regenerate the window from today forward, and leave past occurrences untouched. The trade-off you must name: you accept a background roller and a reconciliation job to gain cheap edits and stable history. No roller means your window silently empties and future reminders stop — a silent failure users notice before your alerts do.
Timezones are a UX problem, not a formatting problem

Users think in wall-clock time: *9am every weekday no matter where I am, or no matter DST*. If you convert to UTC once and discard the timezone, you have silently changed the promise. In fall-back, 09:00 still means 09:00; in spring-forward, a 02:30 daily either does not exist or happens twice. The fix is to store three fields together: `wall_time`, `timezone`, and `anchoring_policy`. Most task products want **floating-by-default with opt-in fixed**: medication reminders stay at 09:00 local when the user flies from Chicago to London; a stock-market open reminder stays pinned to America/New_York. Why retain both? Because UTC alone cannot reconstruct intent after a timezone database update or a user move, and wall-time alone cannot order firings globally. The trade-off: storing intent plus resolved UTC costs a recomputation on every TZDB release and every user move, but it prevents the worst UX bug in scheduling — firing an hour late for a week after DST and looking incompetent.

items: Store `rrule + wall_time + timezone + created_tz_version`. Resolve to UTC at expansion time, not at creation time.
Default to **local wall-clock**: `FREQ=DAILY;BYHOUR=9` in `user_timezone`. Offer `pin_to_timezone` only when the event is anchored to a place.
On user timezone change, ask: **keep 9am local or keep the absolute moment?** Do not guess. Guessing is how you miss flights and medication.
Use IANA names (`America/Chicago`), never offsets (`-05:00`). Offsets cannot survive DST.
Cap expansion in user-local days, then convert. Expanding in UTC shifts daily boundaries for users ahead of UTC.

blocks.title: The 02:30 trap
blocks.text: A daily at **02:30** fails twice a year in most US zones: it does not exist on spring-forward and occurs twice on fall-back. Decide and document: **skip-and-log** vs. **snap-forward to 03:30** vs. **fire once**. Interviewers probe this because it separates people who have shipped from people who have only used cron. Say your policy out loud; any consistent policy beats hand-waving.
Editing, deleting, and skipping: where naive designs die

Creation is 10% of the design. Mutation is 90%. Users edit one instance (*skip this Friday*), this-and-following (*new time from now on*), or the whole series (*delete everything*). If occurrences are just computed dates, you cannot record *skipped* without forking the rule. The production answer is **exceptions as first-class rows**: `Override{series_id, occurrence_id, action: skipped|rescheduled|edited, new_time, new_payload}` that overlay the expansion. Expansion becomes `base_dates(rule) - skipped + rescheduled`. Why this shape? Because it makes the three edit scopes trivial: single-instance writes one override, this-and-following splits the series into two templates at the cut date, all-future rewrites the template and drops window rows after now. The trade-off: reads must merge two sources every time, so you pay a join on calendar fetch to buy O(1) edits that never corrupt history.

Note what this schema buys you for future-proofing: the `rrule` stays RFC-5545 compatible so you can import/export to calendar apps later, `anchoring` lets you add fixed-time semantics without migration, and `end.count` bounds the series so a runaway `FREQ=MINUTELY` cannot DOS your expander. Enforce limits at the API boundary: max occurrences per series, max window size, reject `INTERVAL=1 MINUTELY` without an end. The trade-off is paternalism vs. reliability — power users complain about caps, but one unbounded per-minute series from a script can starve the roller for everyone else. Rate-limit series creation per user and validate expansion cost before accepting the write.
Firing exactly once (enough)

You cannot achieve true exactly-once delivery over a network that can partition, so stop promising it. Promise **exactly-once effect**: fire at least once, deduplicate everywhere else. The pattern is claim-check plus idempotency key. The dispatcher inserts `(occurrence_id, fire_at)` into the delayed queue. Workers acquire a short lease with `UPDATE occurrences SET claimed_by=X, lease_until=now+30s WHERE occurrence_id=Y AND status='due' AND (claimed_by IS NULL OR lease_until < now)`. Only the lease holder sends the push, then marks `fired` with the same `idempotency_key = series_id#date#v1` propagated to the notifier. Retries reuse the key, so a crashed worker that already sent but died before marking still converges to one visible notification. Why a lease and not a delete-from-queue? Because queues redeliver and processes crash between send and ack. The trade-off: you add 30-60 seconds of worst-case duplicate suppression window and a sweeper for orphaned leases, but you eliminate the classic double-push on deploy that destroys trust in reminders.

blocks.title: Occurrence lifecycle
blocks.caption: Leases make double-fire impossible in effect, even when delivery retries.
blocks.code:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Scheduled
  Scheduled --> Due: fire_at reached
  Due --> Claimed: lease acquired
  Claimed --> Fired: notify acked
  Claimed --> Due: lease expired
  Due --> Skipped: override skipped
  Scheduled --> Cancelled: series deleted
  Fired --> [*]

blocks.text: Do not poll the primary schedule table every second from every app server. That query — `WHERE next_fire <= now LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` — works to a few thousand schedules, then becomes a hot row hotspot at the top of every minute and hour. Realistic design uses a two-tier dispatch: a single elected scheduler (or sharded schedulers by `hash(series_id)`) loads the due window and pushes to a delayed queue like SQS delay, Redis sorted set, or Kafka with delayed delivery. App servers only consume. The trade-off is operational: you must run leader election or consistent hashing for the dispatcher tier, but you remove N-way polling thunder and get natural sharding when 09:00 spikes 100x normal load.

blocks.caption: Pick your firing substrate by scale, not by fashion.
rows: DB poll + `SKIP LOCKED`
Under ~10k active schedules, single region, MVP
Minute-boundary hotspot; missed fires if poller stalls; clock skew across pollers
Redis sorted set (`ZADD` fire_at)
Medium scale, need sub-second precision, bursty
Lose persistence unless AOF + replica; big ZRANGEBYLEX on :00 spikes
Delayed queue / scheduler service
High scale, multi-region, need retry + DLQ
More infra; must handle queue redelivery idempotently anyway

blocks.text: How it fails in production

items: **Double notification at deploy:** two workers both think they own `due` because the lease was in memory. Symptom: user gets 09:00 standup twice. Fix: DB-backed lease + downstream idempotency key, not in-memory dedup.

**Silent stop after DST or TZDB update:** resolved UTC times cached in window are now an hour off and never recomputed. Symptom: all reminders an hour late for a week. Fix: version TZDB, recompute window on version bump.

**Midnight thundering herd:** 80% of dailies set for 00:00 or 09:00. Symptom: queue depth explodes, p99 fire latency 4 minutes. Fix: jitter non-critical fires by ±5 min, shard dispatcher, autoscale workers on queue depth — not CPU.

**Orphaned window:** roller crashes, window empties, no new occurrences enqueued. Symptom: no errors, just no reminders. Fix: alert on `min(fire_at) - now < 7 days` per shard; roller is a critical service.
**Edit race:** user reschedules series while occurrence is `claimed`. Symptom: old time still fires. Fix: version the series; claim checks `series_version`, stale claims abort before send.

blocks.text: The midnight spike deserves emphasis because it is an empathy failure disguised as an infra failure. Users pick round times, so load is never uniform — it is a Dirac comb at :00 and :30. If you promise *within a minute* for every reminder, you must provision for that comb or break the promise daily. Mature systems cheat honestly: user-visible countdowns keep exact timing for the next 15 minutes, background dailies get small jitter disclosed in UX as *around 9am*. The trade-off you state in the interview: precision costs capacity. Offer two SLAs — exact for imminent, fuzzy for distant — and save 5-10x workers. That is realistic design, not over-engineering.
What to build for the interview

Do not start with tables. Start with the contract and the edit scopes, then let the schema fall out. Interviewers grading User Empathy want to hear timezone anchoring, skip-vs-delete, and what happens on failure before they hear Kafka vs. Postgres. Draw intent store, expander, delayed queue, and idempotent firer, then go deep on one hard part — usually DST or exactly-once effect — rather than listing every AWS service. The trade-off to voice: breadth impresses juniors, depth convinces seniors.

blocks.code:
from dateutil import rrule, parser
import zoneinfo

def next_occurrences(wall_start: str, tz: str, rule_str: str, after_utc, n=5):
    # Store intent in wall-clock + IANA tz; resolve to UTC at expansion.
    # Trade-off: recompute on every read to survive DST/TZDB changes.
    zone = zoneinfo.ZoneInfo(tz)
    start = parser.isoparse(wall_start).replace(tzinfo=zone)
    rule = rrule.rrulestr(rule_str, dtstart=start)
    # dateutil handles missing 02:30 on spring-forward by shifting forward;
    # log it so UX can disclose "moved to 03:30 due to DST".
    out = []
    for dt in rule.xafter(after_utc, count=n, inc=False):
        occurrence_id = f"ser_9f2#{dt.astimezone(zone).date().isoformat()}"
        idempotency_key = f"{occurrence_id}#v1"  # bump on payload change
        out.append((occurrence_id, dt.isoformat(), idempotency_key))
    return out

items.title: Clarify the promise
items.text: One-shot or recurring? What precision — second, minute, around? What timezone semantics — floating or pinned? What edit scopes — one, following, all? State limits: max frequency, max horizon.

items.title: Define template vs. occurrence
items.text: Draw the two entities and the override table. Show occurrence_id as deterministic. This answers skip, snooze, and history in one move.

items.title: Walk a fire end-to-end
items.text: API → store intent → expand window → delayed queue → lease-claim → idempotent notify. Name the trade-off at each hop: consistency for intent, availability for firing.

items.title: Go deep on one failure
items.text: Pick DST 02:30 or double-fire on deploy. Show lease SQL or idempotency key flow. Explain symptom the user sees, not just the backend log.

items.title: Close with scale and empathy
items.text: Name the 09:00 herd and your jitter SLA, the roller lag alert, and the UX copy for timezone moves. Future-proofing is versioned series + RFC-5545 rules so calendar sync is additive later.

blocks.text: Misconceptions that fail you

items: **Cron is a scheduler.** Cron is a single-box fire list with no leases, no idempotency, no timezone intent. It double-fires on failover and silently skips on downtime. Fine for internal jobs, wrong for user promises.
**Store UTC and forget.** UTC tells you when, never what the user meant. Without wall-time + timezone you cannot survive DST or a user move.
**Exactly-once delivery is achievable.** It is not. Settle for at-least-once delivery plus exactly-once effect via deterministic idempotency keys.
**Materialize the whole series.** A daily with no end is infinite. Materialize a rolling window or one unbounded rule will page you at 3am.
**Polling the DB from every server scales.** It scales until the top of the hour, then every server contends on the same due rows. Shard dispatch, consume from a queue.
**Skipping equals deleting.** Deleting rewrites history and breaks audit. Skipping is an override that preserves the fact the instance existed and was intentionally missed.

blocks.text: When to use it and when not to

blocks.caption: Match the machinery to the promise you actually made.
rows: User-visible reminders, tasks, calendar events
Internal cron that can slip 10 minutes unnoticed
Human trust needs leases and idempotency; internal jobs need simplicity
Recurrence with edits, skips, timezone moves
Fixed one-shot webhooks with no edits
Overrides and templates only pay off when mutation is frequent
Scale past one box or past one region
Prototype with <1k schedules
Dispatcher + queue is operational overhead; DB poll wins under 10k
Need audit / history / snooze / analytics
Fire-and-forget emails
Per-occurrence rows give you state to query; otherwise they are dead weight

blocks.title: What to say in one sentence if asked
blocks.text: Store **user intent as rule plus wall-clock plus timezone**, expand a **bounded window** merged with **overrides**, and fire via **leased claims with idempotent keys** — so edits stay cheap, DST stays correct, and retries never double-notify.
